I've been using Linux and ATI/AMD/Nvidia for a long time. Since my x800 Pro and 8800 GTS 320MB. AMD used to be terrible, fglrx still is pretty bad. But the open source drivers, even the "old" radeonhd one, works great. You do take a little performance hit, but it's completely stable and it just works. Running radeonhd for years in Gentoo, I've never had to mess with config files or had anything broken. It's come a very, very long way. Not to mention it has native DX9 support for older games via WINE, something you won't get via proprietary driver. GPGPU isn't there yet (which might kill it for you, specially if you use Blender), but the Russians are working on it. https://www.x.org/wiki/RadeonFeature/

I'm aware AMD is now focusing on the AMDGPU driver instead of the radeon one, but the radeon one is still being actively developed by third parties, like all good open source software is. I try and avoid proprietary software anywhere in Linux, when it comes to Nvidia driver. Nvidia open source is awful, most of the time it's flat out broken, so you have to use Nvidia proprietary driver. Nvidia has a history of keeping up to date with xorg releases and stuff, but even so, you're depending on Nvidia to keep your card working entirely. A company that recently gimped Kepler performance in some games in order to coerce them to upgrade to Maxwell. Not to mention you always have to fight closed source software in Linux. It just doesn't belong there. It's always caused me problems, whether it's a NIC, WIFI, or graphics card.

Going forward, the only option for AMD once they release cards will be their hybrid open source driver. It's going to be a mostly open source and free (as in freedom) driver that's backed and developed by AMD as well as the community. Given how well radeonhd (I run the southern islands version) has improved over time, I'm really optimistic.

I've been using ATI (in Windows at least) since Rage 128 Pro, and Nvidia on and off since Geforce 4 MX 440. I have a lot of experience with both. My honest opinion? ATI/AMD drivers started way behind Nvidia and eventually caught up, I think they're basically at the point where they're neck and neck. They both are having problems, Nvidia keeps releasing drivers that kill cards, AMD still has some game support problems and it will do some stupid stuff like move your desktop icons when you install drivers. But my point is that about three or more years ago, there was a huge difference between the two. Now, it's not so much, on either Linux or Windows.

To me, it's the choice between Nvidia proprietary driver or AMD open source. But being at Nvidia's mercy of hoping they don't drop support for my old card (they dropped Fermi Vulkan support recently even though they said they never would, because "there's not enough users for it to be worth their time" http://wccftech.com/nvidia-fermi-geforce-400-500-vulkan-api-support/), when that's not the case with open source drivers, it seems to me like even a little performance loss is worth it.

I run open source radeon drivers on my A4-5000 laptop too. It can pull around 8 hours of video playback with the screen turned down low. Power management has improved a lot, and IIRC correctly it's even using an old kernel with old radeon drivers, 3.x version of the kernel. Power management was also improved with the latest driver.

I know this is not going to be a popular post, lots of people have had bad experiences with AMD and ATI, specially in Linux. But things have gotten better. I remember fighting xorg with black screens of death on xorg starting for days. Now I find it pretty easy to switch between fglrx and radeonhd on Gentoo.

Would love to upvoat you more than once if I could. Answer as it should be, backed by experience and not just fanboyism. Also thanks for getting the facts straight; this explains a lot about my personal experience. Cheers.
